newsitem.title: DUBAI: Truce slows exodus of refugees from northern Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Truce slows exodus of refugees from northern Iraq.

text.p: A U.S.-brokered ceasefire in northern Iraq has slowed the exodus of Kurdish refugees into Iran, where tens of thousands of Iraqi Kurds are taking refuge, a U.N. official said on Tuesday.

But Laurens Jolles, an official of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Tehran, said that despite last week's truce, the refugees at several camps in Iran were not rushing back home.

"Fewer refugees have come to Iran and some who were on the Iraqi side of the border are no longer there, they seem to have returned," he told Reuters by telephone, referring to 1,200 refugees that Iran said on Saturday were waiting to cross the border into Iran.
"But the truce is very recent and most people's attitude is wait and see. The situation there (in northern Iraq) is fluid," Jolles added. "We are not talking about a significant return of refugees."
The rival Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) had agreed to observe the U.S.-mediated ceasefire last week halting two months of fighting.
Western relief groups said on Monday 15,000 new refugees had arrived in Iran since October 18 and that little food or water was available to the refugees, living in cold mountain camps.
Jolles said the living conditions of the estimated 60,000 Kurdish refugees sheltering in Iran were "really bad" due to the below zero temperatures and rain.
The Iranian government has repeatedly complained of receiving little international funds to look after the refugees.
Jolles said the U.N. has already given Iran $3 million.
Iran is home to two million refugees, 1.4 million from Afghanistan and 600,000 from Iraq, making it the world's most important host country, according to UNHCR.
